title: Christian Eschatology Position Matrix
purpose: Prevent the archive from treating one end-times timetable as Christianity as a whole by comparing major Christian confessional and interpretive families across return, resurrection, judgment, rapture, tribulation, millennium and new creation.
common_center: Across many major Christian traditions, a broad common center is that Jesus Christ returns, the dead are raised, judgment occurs and God's final purpose is consummated. Traditions disagree substantially about sequence, millennium, tribulation, Israel/church relations and the interpretation of apocalyptic texts.

positions.return_of_christ: Jesus Christ comes again in glory.
positions.visibility/personality: The creed identifies the returning subject as Jesus Christ himself.
positions.resurrection: Resurrection of the dead / body is part of the final hope.
positions.judgment: Christ judges the living and the dead.
positions.rapture: No detailed secret-rapture timetable is defined by the Nicene Creed.
positions.new_creation: Life of the world to come.

positions.return_of_christ: Christ's return precedes final consummation and judgment.
positions.visibility/personality: The returning Christ is the same Jesus Christ of Christian confession.
positions.resurrection: General resurrection is part of final judgment and consummation.
positions.rapture: Catholic doctrine does not adopt the standard dispensational secret pre-tribulation rapture scheme as its eschatological framework.
positions.tribulation: The Catechism teaches a final trial of the Church and warns of pseudo-messianic deception.
positions.millennium: The Catechism rejects millenarian attempts to realize final messianic hope inside history in the condemned sense it describes.
positions.new_creation: God's final victory and consummation beyond merely historical political triumph.

positions.return_of_christ: Christ comes again in glory at the end of the ages.
positions.visibility/personality: The same Christ who ascended returns; his presence is itself judgment.
positions.resurrection: All are raised from the dead.
positions.judgment: Christ judges humanity, with strong emphasis on lived relation to God and neighbor.
positions.rapture: 1 Thessalonians 4's caught-up language is read within the final coming rather than as a separate modern dispensational timetable.
positions.tribulation: Not normally organized as the popular secret-rapture chart system.
positions.millennium: Mainstream Orthodox theology does not center a literal earthly millennial timetable as the core of eschatology.
positions.new_creation: Material creation itself is understood as renewed and glorified rather than simply discarded.

positions.return_of_christ: At the consummation Christ appears for judgment.
positions.visibility/personality: One final return of Christ rather than a separate invisible return followed by another visible return in classical confessional teaching.
positions.judgment: The godly receive eternal life; the ungodly are condemned in the classical confession.
positions.rapture: Contemporary LCMS teaching accepts 1 Thessalonians 4's catching-up while rejecting a separate invisible pre-tribulation coming.
positions.tribulation: Not the organizing center of Augsburg Confession Article XVII.
positions.millennium: The Augsburg Confession rejects specific Jewish-style earthly-kingdom expectations it encountered; Lutheran traditions generally do not center dispensational premillennialism.
positions.new_creation: Final eternal life belongs to the consummation rather than an endlessly deferred earthly scheme.
positions.date_setting: No date-setting authority is supplied by the confession.

positions.resurrection: Bodies are raised and reunited with souls in the confession's framework.
positions.judgment: A final day of judgment is strongly affirmed.
positions.rapture: The Westminster Standards do not define the later dispensational pre-tribulation rapture system.
positions.tribulation: Views vary among Reformed Christians; not one required detailed timetable in the Westminster Confession.
positions.millennium: Reformed Christians have included amillennial, postmillennial and some premillennial readings; the confession itself does not function as a dispensational chart.
positions.new_creation: Final blessedness and judgment belong to the consummation.
positions.date_setting: The timing is not given for speculative calculation.

positions.return_of_christ: Christ returns and judges the living and dead; new creation is part of the final horizon.
positions.resurrection: Affirmed within the broader Christian doctrinal tradition.
positions.rapture: The UMC states that rapture and Great-Tribulation schemes are not part of its doctrinal standards.
positions.tribulation: No required dispensational Great Tribulation timetable.
positions.millennium: No single detailed end-times 'ism' is made the practical center of official teaching.
positions.new_creation: Strongly emphasized in Methodist explanation of the Second Coming.
positions.date_setting: Speculative date calculation is discouraged in practice.

positions.return_of_christ: Jesus Christ returns personally and visibly in glory.
positions.visibility/personality: Personal and visible return of Jesus Christ.
positions.rapture: The Baptist Faith and Message does not prescribe one detailed rapture timetable even though many individual Baptists hold dispensational views.
positions.tribulation: Not fixed by the confession's concise Last Things article.
positions.millennium: Not fixed by that article; Baptist churches and theologians vary.
positions.new_creation: Final destiny of righteous and unrighteous is affirmed.
positions.date_setting: God acts 'in His own time and in His own way.'

positions.return_of_christ: Typically distinguishes a catching-away of the church from a later public return of Christ, depending on the specific dispensational school.
positions.visibility/personality: Christ remains the returning subject; sequence is divided more sharply than in many older confessional traditions.
positions.resurrection: Often organized into stages within the dispensational timetable.
positions.judgment: Multiple judgment moments may be distinguished.
positions.rapture: Usually central; classic popular forms are pre-tribulation.
positions.tribulation: A defined future tribulation is normally central.
positions.millennium: Future literal millennium after Christ's return is central.
positions.new_creation: Follows the millennial and final-judgment sequence in standard schemes.
positions.date_setting: Responsible dispensational theologians do not need to endorse date-setting; popular movements have sometimes done so.
positions.historical_note: Modern dispensationalism was powerfully shaped by John Nelson Darby and later popularizers such as C. I. Scofield, but historical development is more complex than saying one person invented every component.
positions.scholarship: Crawford Gribben, J. N. Darby and the Roots of Dispensationalism (Oxford University Press, 2024).

positions.resurrection: Resurrection is closely tied to Christ's return.
positions.judgment: Final judgment remains part of the consummation.
positions.rapture: Does not require a separate secret pre-tribulation rapture in the dispensational sense.
positions.tribulation: Often expects the church to experience end-time tribulation rather than be removed before it.
positions.millennium: Future millennial reign after Christ returns.
positions.new_creation: Final new creation follows the eschatological consummation.

positions.return_of_christ: One climactic return of Christ at the end of the age.
positions.resurrection: General resurrection associated with final consummation.
positions.judgment: Final judgment follows or coincides with the return/resurrection complex.
positions.rapture: 1 Thessalonians 4 is commonly read as believers meeting the arriving Lord rather than disappearing years before a later return.
positions.tribulation: Can be read as the church's recurring/end-time suffering rather than a rigid seven-year chart.
positions.millennium: Revelation 20's millennium is usually interpreted symbolically as the present reign of Christ or church age.
positions.new_creation: Follows the final return and judgment.

positions.return_of_christ: Christ returns after a long period of gospel success / millennial blessing as defined by the school.
positions.rapture: A separate secret pre-tribulation rapture is not inherent to postmillennialism.
positions.tribulation: Not necessarily organized as a future seven-year dispensational period.
positions.millennium: A long era of Christian flourishing or kingdom influence precedes the final return.

positions.return_of_christ: The Second Coming is a central, literal, personal and visible hope in Adventist doctrine.
positions.visibility/personality: Jesus Christ returns personally and visibly.
positions.resurrection: The righteous dead are raised in connection with the return; Adventism has a distinctive sequence for later resurrection/judgment themes.
positions.judgment: Judgment is a major doctrinal category with distinctive Adventist sanctuary/investigative-judgment teaching.
positions.rapture: Adventism does not teach the standard secret pre-tribulation rapture model.
positions.tribulation: End-time conflict is important but not organized according to classic dispensational separation of church and Israel.
positions.millennium: A literal thousand-year period is affirmed within a distinct Adventist sequence.
positions.new_creation: New earth follows the final resolution of sin and judgment.
positions.date_setting: The movement historically emerged from failed date expectation and official teaching rejects setting a date for Christ's return.

interpretive_lenses.summary: Emphasizes fulfillment in the ancient historical context, especially the first centuries and Roman imperial setting.
Maps apocalyptic visions across long sequences of church and world history.
Places much apocalyptic fulfillment near the end of history.
Reads apocalyptic images as recurring theological patterns of empire, witness, conflict, judgment and divine victory.
Combines ancient context, recurring symbolism and future consummation.

potatoverse_use.rule: Before calling an event 'the Second Coming', 'the rapture', 'the tribulation' or 'the millennium', identify which Christian interpretive framework is being invoked and whether the Potatoverse is claiming identity, typology, analogy or a new doctrine.
potatoverse_use.important_difference: Potatoverse rupture is not a standard Christian technical term and should remain separate from rapture.
potatoverse_use.comparison_value: The matrix lets readers see whether a Tim/Thomas interpretation resembles Nicene common ground, Lutheran eschatology, dispensational futurism, idealist Revelation reading, or another framework rather than vaguely saying 'Christianity says'.

sources.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000 — Last Things
Crawford Gribben — J. N. Darby and the Roots of Dispensationalism
